desc: Founded by Steven Greer in 1993 as an offshoot of his Center for the Study of Extraterrestrial Intelligence, the Disclosure Project's method was to locate former military, intelligence, contractor and air traffic personnel with first-hand UFO experience, record their testimony on video, and use the aggregate to demand congressional hearings with subpoena power and witness amnesty. It briefed members of Congress and officials in Washington in April 1997 - the same week the Wilson-Davis notes later record as the trigger for Admiral Wilson's inquiries - and staged its major public event at the National Press Club on 9 May 2001 with roughly twenty witnesses and a stated corpus of more than four hundred. No hearing followed. The project's structural contribution is the demonstration that witness aggregation without documents does not move institutions: the 2001 event produced global coverage and zero congressional action, whereas the 2023 Grusch testimony - one witness with an Inspector General complaint, a security clearance and a statutory whistleblower channel - produced a hearing. The lesson the modern movement learned from Greer is that the paperwork is the lever.

dossier.narrative:
The Disclosure Project's importance to this board is structural rather than evidential. Its Briefing Document is the anchor under a large share of the witness claims the board carries, which is why the document has its own L0 node, and its 2001 press conference is the event most often invoked as the moment those claims entered public life.

Two documented facts complicate it, and the node carries both. It controlled access to its own press events: Klass records being refused admission to a comparable 1997 conference, and reportedly the Fund for UFO Research was refused too. An organisation that selects its audience is entitled to, and a board recording its output should note it. And the Clinton White House's principal UFO FOIA collection, 2006-0474-F, consists in the majority of documents sent to the White House by Greer of CSETI, which means a federal records collection frequently cited as government material is substantially this organisation's own correspondence arriving back through the front door.

Its reach is not only rhetorical. The Wilson-Davis notes record the Disclosure Project's April 1997 Washington briefing week as the proximate trigger for Admiral Thomas Wilson's attempt to locate a special access programme. Whatever one concludes about the testimony, the organisation demonstrably moved a senior officer to go looking, and the board carries that at Tier 3 because the notes themselves are contested.

The 19 September pass found the organisation's cross-referencing habit worth flagging: the compiler links his own witnesses to each other in editorial notes, so convergence inside the Briefing Document is not independent convergence.

dossier.whatItIs: A private witness-aggregation and congressional-hearing campaign founded by Steven M. Greer, running from 1993, whose method is to interview former military and government personnel on video and publish summarised transcripts. Its April 2001 Briefing Document prints sixty-eight dated testimonies; its press conference of 9 May 2001 presented about twenty witnesses and called for congressional hearings with subpoena power and amnesty.
dossier.whyImplicated: It is the largest single upstream source of witness claims on this board, and it is also an interested party with an explicit political objective. Both facts have to be visible at once. The board carries its testimony because the testimony is dated and attributed, and grades that testimony carefully because the collection method is one man with a stated goal.
